# Vattha Sutta (MN 7 (PTS MN i 36))

**ID:** MN 7 (PTS MN i 36)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Vattha Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Simile of the Cloth
**PTS:** MN i 36
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn7
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vattha Sutta* (also known as the *Vatthūpama Sutta*, "The Simile of the Cloth") opens with the analogy of a soiled cloth that cannot be successfully dyed versus a clean cloth that absorbs dye evenly: similarly, a mind defiled by corruptions leads to a miserable destination, whereas an undefiled mind attains joy and higher states of consciousness [SuttaCentral; Human Nature and Conflict]. The sutta enumerates sixteen corruptions of the mind (*upakkilesa*), including pairs such as anger and revenge, contempt and arrogance, envy and avarice, and deceit and fraudulence [Bodhi 2003; Rogell 2003]. It describes the arising of unwavering confidence through recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha (specifically praising the noble disciples as comprising the "four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals") [Human Nature and Conflict; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Apple 2008]. It further details the development of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) and the realization that there is an escape beyond the whole realm of perception (*saññāgata*) [Buddhist Philosophy and Meditation Practice 2012; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. In the closing section, the Buddha addresses the brāhmaṇa Sundarika Bhāradvāja, rejecting the Brahmanical belief that ritual bathing in sacred rivers (such as the Phaggu) can wash away sins; hearing the discourse, the brāhmaṇa goes for refuge, receives monastic ordination, and attains arahantship [SuttaCentral; Bapat and Hirakawa 1970; Sujato 2012].

Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral include versions in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 93), *Ekottarika Āgama* (EĀ 13.5), *Saṃyukta Āgama* (SĀ 1185 and SĀ² 98 / T 100), and an individual translation, T 51 [SuttaCentral]. Unlike MN 7, in MĀ 93 Sundarika Bhāradvāja only takes refuge as a lay follower rather than becoming an ordained monk [Sujato 2012]. DharmaNexus corroborates these cross-language alignments with T 125, T 99, T 100, and T 51, and identifies additional alignments with Sanskrit (Vīryaśrīdatta's *Arthaviniścayasūtra-nibandhana*) and Tibetan texts (*Udānavargavivaraṇa*, *Vinayavastu*) [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records 1,193 text-reuse matches across 137 texts, sharing extensive segments with AN 4, AN 3, the *Upakkilesa Sutta* (MN 128, on the mental corruptions), the *Brāhmaṇa Saṃyutta* (SN 7, on the Sundarika verses), AN 11, SN 55, and MN 83 [DharmaNexus].
